title: Introduction and Complex Systems Concepts
reading:
## 1. Course overview

- **Topics across the semester:** what a complex system is; modelling of complex systems; cellular automata; network models; agent-based models; training complex systems with evolutionary algorithms; the brain as a complex system (biological neurons, biological learning, artificial neural networks); agentic AI ecosystems; bonus material.
- **Group project:** a delivery consisting of a report and code. It counts **50 %** of the final grade. The report must be **10-15 pages**. Both the code/program and the report are evaluated. Groups of **2-3 students** (exceptions in special cases). Some lectures are used as practical "lab sessions". Project topics and the deadline are published on Canvas.
- **Textbook:** Sayama, *Introduction to the Modeling and Analysis of Complex Systems* (free, open source; <https://bingdev.binghamton.edu/sayama/textbook/>). Only some parts are used: chapters 1, 2, 10; CA = 11; networks = 15, 16, 17; ABM = 19. Exercises are on the book website. Code examples: **PyCX** (<https://github.com/hsayama/PyCX>, old site <http://pycx.sourceforge.net/>).
- **Intro material on the slides:** the *Complexity Explained* project (<https://complexityexplained.github.io/>, De Domenico, Brockmann, Camargo, Gershenson, Goldsmith, Jeschonnek, Kay, Nichele, Nicolás, Schmickl, Stella, Brandoff, Martínez Salinas, Sayama, 2019, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/TQGNW), a YouTube video, and a bonus paper (arXiv 2608.10218).

## 2. What is a complex system?

**Simple systems sit at two opposite extremes:**

- **Completely correlated parts**, for example a mechanical watch: every gear is tightly linked to every other gear.
- **Totally independent parts**, for example rolling dice: each die has nothing to do with the others.

Complex systems live **between** these two extremes. Their parts are neither fully locked together nor fully independent.

**Definition (from the slides):**

> Complex systems are networks made of a number of components that interact with each other, typically in a nonlinear fashion. Complex systems may arise and evolve through self-organization, such that they are neither completely regular nor completely random, permitting the development of emergent behavior at macroscopic scales.

**Two key concepts:**

- **Emergence:** some property of a system observed at macroscopic scales is difficult to explain by the microscopic rules that drive the system. There is a non-trivial relationship between the system's properties at different scales. (Emergence happens **over scale**.)
- **Self-organization:** the system spontaneously organizes itself, over time, to produce non-trivial macroscopic behaviour. (Self-organization happens **over time**.)

**Summary of what makes a system complex:**

- Small, "simple" components
- Locally correlated and interacting parts
- Self-organization (over time)
- Emergence (over scale)
- "The whole is more than the sum of its parts" (Aristotle)

**Examples of self-organization:**

- **Magnetization:** individual magnetic spins start randomly oriented but, under the right conditions, spontaneously align into ordered domains.
- **Bénard rolls:** a fluid heated from below spontaneously organizes into rolling convection cells instead of conducting heat chaotically.

**Properties of complex systems:**

- **Non-linearity:** small changes in input do not give proportionally small changes in output.
- **Bifurcation (chaos):** when a control parameter (for example the temperature difference) crosses a critical threshold, the system's behaviour can split into qualitatively different stable states (for example convection rolling clockwise vs. counter-clockwise).

## 3. Modelling: the scientific cycle and its pitfall

**Science** tries to understand the world by discovering fundamental laws that describe how it works.

**The naive scientific cycle:**

1. Observe a phenomenon **P**.
2. Come up with a hypothesis **H** that explains P (H → P is always true, because you chose H that way).
3. Derive a prediction **Q** from H (H → Q).
4. Run an experiment to see whether Q is observed.
   - If **not Q**, then H is wrong. Go back and formulate a new hypothesis.
   - If **Q is observed**, this tells you *nothing* about whether H is true. Your hypothesis could still be wrong or insufficient.

**The logical flaw:** this is the fallacy of *affirming the consequent*. Obtaining supportive evidence does not prove your hypothesis. You only failed to disprove it, which makes it a *well-tested* hypothesis, never a proven one.

**What a model is:**

- A **model** is a simplified representation of a system (verbal, conceptual, diagrammatic, physical, formal or mathematical).
- We (cognitive beings) build models in our minds all the time.
- **Engineering** is the effort to control or influence nature (or a system) so that something desirable happens, by creating and controlling models.

**Two families of modelling approaches:**

| Approach | Goal | Captures |
|---|---|---|
| **Descriptive modelling** | Specify the actual state of a system at one or more points in time. Examples: a photo, a miniature, a biography, regression, statistics, pattern recognition. | What the system *looks like* |
| **Rule-based modelling** | Find dynamical rules that explain observed behaviour and predict future states. Examples: dynamical equations, first-principles theories, Darwin's theory of evolution. | How the system *will behave* |

**The rule-based modelling cycle:**

1. Observe the system of interest.
2. Reflect on possible rules that could cause the observed characteristics.
3. Derive predictions from those rules and compare them with reality.
4. Repeat and refine until satisfied (or until you run out of time or funding).

This avoids the "hypothesis proven" trap because the goal is refinement, not proof. But it has its own hard step: **coming up with the right rules (step 2) is fundamentally difficult.** It is a personal process that depends on your knowledge, your cognitive thinking and your experience. There is no algorithm for it.

**Why complex systems are especially hard to model:**

- They have unique properties: networks, non-linearity, emergence, self-organization.
- This pushes modelling toward **computational modelling and simulation** and **AI models (machine learning)**, because closed-form analytical models are often infeasible.

## 4. What comes next in the course

Interactive simulation of complex systems; cellular automata models; network models; agent-based models; evolutionary systems; and so on.

## 5. Exam focus for Lecture 1

- Explain simple vs. complex systems (watch vs. dice).
- Define complex system, self-organization, emergence, and say which goes with time and which with scale.
- Give examples of self-organization (magnetization, Bénard rolls) and explain non-linearity and bifurcation.
- Explain the logical flaw in the naive scientific cycle (affirming the consequent).
- Compare descriptive and rule-based modelling and describe the rule-based cycle.
- Say why step 2 (finding rules) is hard and why complex systems push us to simulation and AI.

> **Note on a simplified version:** the original chat also contains a second, beginner-friendly explanation of this lecture (analogies: watches vs. dice, ant colonies, heated liquid forming rolling patterns), written because the content felt too technical on the first pass. That version is not reproduced here.

title: Interactive Simulation of Complex Systems and Introduction to Cellular Automata
reading:
## 1. Complex systems (recap)

A complex system has these characteristics:

- Many small, "simple" components.
- Locally correlated and interacting parts.
- **Self-organization** is order that appears *over time*, without central control.
- **Emergence** is properties that appear *over scale*. They exist at the macro level but not in the individual parts.
- "The whole is more than the sum of its parts" (Aristotle).

Examples on the slides: crowds of people, the internet, networks, neurons and ants.

**Core question:** what happens when you have a huge number of dynamical components that interact in nontrivial ways? Emergence and self-organization follow from a system being made of a massive amount of interacting components.

**Exam tip:** self-organization goes with time, emergence with scale. It is easy to swap them.

## 2. Interactive simulation with PyCX

PyCX is a library of Python examples (<https://github.com/hsayama/PyCX>). The workflow is *run, change parameters, re-run*. Every model has the same three functions: initialize, observe, update.

```python
import pycxsimulator
from pylab import *

def initialize():
    global ...        # set the initial state
def observe():
    global ...
    cla()             # clears the visualization space
    ...               # visualize the state
def update():
    global ...        # one discrete time step

pycxsimulator.GUI().start(func=[initialize, observe, update])
```

**Exercise 10.6** is a random-walk particle model. There are n = 1000 particles, and each gets Gaussian noise `normal(0, sd)` in x and y per time step, with sd = 0.1. Initial positions are drawn from `normal(0, 1)`. `observe` plots with `plot(xlist, ylist, '.', alpha=0.2)`.

**Interactive parameter control** uses a *parameter setter*:

```python
def num_particles(val = n):
    '''Number of particles. Change while the simulation is not running, then reset.'''
    global n
    n = int(val)
    return val

pycxsimulator.GUI(parameterSetters=[num_particles]).start(func=[initialize, observe, update])
```

- The docstring is shown as the description in the GUI.
- `n` must be changed while the simulation is stopped, and then reset. Otherwise you get an error, because the lists have the wrong length.

**Exercise 10.2** (add a setter for `sd`):

```python
def sd_param(val = sd):
    '''Standard deviation of Gaussian noise.'''
    global sd
    sd = float(val)      # float, not int
    return val

pycxsimulator.GUI(parameterSetters=[num_particles, sd_param]).start(func=[initialize, observe, update])
```

`sd` can be changed mid-run without a reset, because it does not change the data structures.

**Simulation without PyCX** means calling the functions yourself:

```python
t = 0
initialize(); observe()
for t in range(1, 100):
    update(); observe()    # observe can e.g. call savefig(str(t)+'.png')
```

## 3. Cellular Automata (CA)

### What and why

- An **automaton** is a theoretical machine that changes its internal state based on inputs and its previous state.
- A **CA** is a set of such automata arranged on a regular spatial grid. All cells are updated **simultaneously** by the **same** state-transition function, which only looks at neighbour states.
- A CA is the "simplest possible universe capable of computation". Space is a D-dimensional grid of cells (D = 1, 2, 3), and **time and space are discrete**.
- The rules are also called an FSM (finite state machine).
- CA were invented by **John von Neumann** (1940s) to study biological self-replication in machines and universal computers with simple rules. *Theory of Self-Reproducing Automata* was completed by Arthur Burks in 1966.
- **Applications:** molecular dynamics, hydrodynamics, physical properties of materials, reaction-diffusion chemical processes, growth and morphogenesis, ecology and evolution of populations, traffic jams, social and economic dynamics. Computational uses: image processing, random number generation, cryptography.
- The state-transition function can be a lookup table, a mathematical formula, a higher-level algorithm or a neural network.
- Slide example: CA modelling two species of gastropod (Chris King, University of Auckland).

### Formal definition

A CA model consists of identical automata (cells or sites) uniformly arranged on lattice points in a D-dimensional discrete space (usually D = 1, 2 or 3). Each automaton is a dynamical variable whose temporal change is given by:

```
s_{t+1}(x) = F( s_t(x + x_0), s_t(x + x_1), ..., s_t(x + x_{n-1}) )
```

- `s_t(x)` is the state of the cell at position x at time t.
- `F` is the **state-transition function**.
- `N = {x_0, ..., x_{n-1}}` is the **neighbourhood**. It is usually centred on the cell (x_0 = 0) and local: |x_i - x_0| <= r, where r is the **radius**.
- `s_t` as a whole (a map from position to state) is called a **configuration**, the spatial pattern the CA shows at time t.
- Assuming spatial regularity and homogeneity was a reasonable first step because von Neumann had no empirical data on how real-world systems are connected. This is extended later with network models.

### 2D neighbourhoods

| Type | Cells (incl. centre) | Which |
|---|---|---|
| **von Neumann** | 5 | C, T, B, L, R (only up/down/left/right) |
| **Moore** | 9 | the 8 surrounding cells plus the centre |

### Properties

- A **quiescent** cell stays in the same state if all its neighbours are quiescent. Anything else is **active**.
- **Boundary conditions:**
  - *No boundaries:* infinite space filled with quiescent cells.
  - *Periodic:* wrap around.
  - *Cut-off:* no neighbours at the edge.
  - *Fixed:* a fixed state at the edge.
- **Totalistic CA:** the transition depends only on the *sum* of the cells in the neighbourhood.

### 1D: elementary CA and Rule 90

- Each cell has two neighbours (radius 1), so there are 2^3 = 8 possible neighbourhood configurations. Each maps to 0 or 1, giving 2^8 = **256 elementary CA**.
- The rule number is the output bits read as a binary number. Neighbourhoods are listed from 111 down to 000.
- **Rule 90** (Wolfram, 1983): 90 = (01011010)_2 = 0·2^7 + 1·2^6 + 0·2^5 + 1·2^4 + 1·2^3 + 0·2^2 + 1·2^1 + 0·2^0.
  - Outputs for 111, 110, 101, 100, 011, 010, 001, 000 are 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0.
  - This equals **left XOR right**. A single 1 grows into a Sierpinski triangle.

### 2D rule examples

1. **Majority (voting) rule:** the next state is the majority in the neighbourhood. The system **self-organizes into geographically separated patches** (Fig. 11.4, Moore).
2. **Parity (XOR) rule:** s_{t+1}(x) = (sum of s_t(x + x_i)) mod k. **Any pattern in the initial configuration replicates and propagates** (Fig. 11.5, von Neumann).
3. **Game of Life** (John Conway, Moore neighbourhood):
   - An alive cell with fewer than 2 alive neighbours dies (*loneliness*).
   - An alive cell with more than 3 alive neighbours dies (*overcrowding*).
   - An alive cell with 2 or 3 alive neighbours lives on (*happiness*).
   - A dead cell with exactly 3 alive neighbours comes alive (*reproduction*). Otherwise it stays dead.

### Slide exercises, solved

**Exercise 11.1** (1D totalistic, radius 1, periodic, 16 cells, new state = round(S/3)):

- S = 0 or 1 gives 0, and S = 2 or 3 gives 1. This is the majority rule.
- States (1 = gray), grouped in fours:

```
t=0  1011 0010 1100 1010
t=1  0111 0001 1100 0101
t=2  1111 0001 1100 0010
t=3  1111 0001 1100 0001
t=4  1111 0001 1100 0001   (fixed point)
```

This is an example of self-organization into stable blocks.

**Exercise 11.2** (2D totalistic, von Neumann, infinite space, new state = round(S/5)):

- S = 0, 1, 2 gives 0, and S = 3, 4, 5 gives 1. A cell becomes 1 when at least 3 of its 5 cells are 1.
- The starting configuration is an "H" of 7 cells.
- **t=1:** a plus shape (centre plus the four neighbours, 5 cells).
- **t=2:** only the centre cell.
- **t=3:** empty. A lone cell has S = 1 and dies, so everything is back in the quiescent state.

## 4. What you should be able to do at the exam

- Define complex system, self-organization and emergence, and tell them apart.
- Explain initialize / observe / update and what a parameter setter is.
- Define a CA (cells, grid, neighbourhood, state set, transition function, discrete time and space) and explain the formula.
- Explain the difference between von Neumann and Moore neighbourhoods, and the four boundary conditions.
- Compute a CA by hand, explain why there are 2^8 elementary rules, and say what 90 means in binary.
- Know the majority, parity and Game of Life rules and the behaviour each produces.
- Know the history: von Neumann (self-replication), Burks (1966), Wolfram (1983), Conway.

**Next on the slides:** more cellular automata; network theory and network models; agent-based models and evolutionary systems; the brain and biological neural network models. Bonus: <https://oimo.io/works/life/>.

> **Note:** the first version of this review was written in Norwegian; the student then asked for the identical review and quiz in English because the exam is likely in English. Only the English version is reproduced here. The student also shared a Notion page with personal notes on this lecture; Claude's suggested additions to those notes (CA formal definition, neighbourhoods/boundaries, Rule 90, the three example rules, PyCX content, the two worked exercises, historical details) are all covered above.

options.c: Only the two cells directly left and right of the original cell

options.c: 0, because S = 2 and round(2/3) = 0
options.d: 1, because both neighbors are 1 and the center is ignored

options.a: Any initial pattern replicates and propagates
options.b: It self-organizes into geographically separated patches of 0s and 1s
options.c: It stays random forever
options.d: It always dies out to all 0s

questions.explanation: Majority rule smooths out disagreement locally, so uniform patches form and stabilize. Option A describes the parity (XOR) rule.

questions.prompt: In Conway's Game of Life, what happens to an alive cell with 4 alive neighbors, and to a dead cell with exactly 3 alive neighbors?

options.a: Alive cell dies (overcrowding); dead cell comes alive (reproduction)
options.b: Alive cell lives on; dead cell stays dead
options.c: Alive cell dies (loneliness); dead cell stays dead
options.d: Alive cell lives on (happiness); dead cell comes alive

reading:
## 1. The Hugging Face incident (motivation slide)

Sources on the slide: OpenAI's post "Hugging Face incident and the road ahead", METR's investigation (2026-08-26), and a LessWrong post on the origins of altruistic behaviour in the incident.

Two concerns about collectives of AI agents:

1. A swarm's capabilities can **grow with its size**, even if each agent is individually limited.
2. A collective can become **misaligned even when every constituent is perfectly aligned**.

**Exam angle:** both are examples of **emergence**, where the global behaviour is not a property of the parts.

## 2. CA simulation: the droplet / panic model

- **Story:** panic spreading among people sitting in a gym after a fire alarm.
- **Rule (Moore neighbourhood, 8 neighbours):**
  - A normal individual becomes panicky if surrounded by **>= 4** panicky individuals.
  - A panicky individual stays panicky if surrounded by **>= 3** panicky individuals. Otherwise it reverts to normal.
- **Assumptions:** 2-D n x n grid (n = 100), **periodic** boundary, random initial condition (panicky with probability *p*, normal with 1 - *p*).
- **Moore neighbourhood:** {(x', y') | x-1 <= x' <= x+1, y-1 <= y' <= y+1}.

**The code (pycxsimulator), three functions:**

- `initialize()` fills `config` randomly with 1 if `random() < p`, and makes an empty `nextconfig`.
- `observe()` draws the grid with `imshow`.
- `update()` loops over all cells and counts over dx, dy in {-1, 0, 1}, using `% n` for **periodic boundaries**. It writes `nextconfig[x,y] = 1 if count >= 4 else 0`, then swaps `config, nextconfig = nextconfig, config`.

Three things the code shows, all likely exam points:

- `nextconfig` is a second buffer, so the update is **synchronous**. Every cell reads the old state.
- The count loop **includes the cell itself**. So `count >= 4` means ">= 4 panicky neighbours" for a normal cell, and ">= 3 panicky neighbours" for a panicky one (3 neighbours + itself = 4). One threshold implements both rules.
- `% n` implements the periodic boundary (the grid wraps like a torus).

**Results:**

- **p = 0.1:** after 20 steps only a few small, stable clusters ("droplets") remain.
- **p = 0.3:** clusters grow, **attach to each other**, and growth becomes unstoppable. The whole space eventually fills with panicky people.
- The switch between these behaviours happens in a **narrow range of p**. That is a **phase transition**: *a transition of macroscopic properties of a collective system that occurs when its environmental or internal conditions are varied.*

**Exercises on the slides:**

- **11.3:** modify the code to simulate Game of Life from a random start.
- **11.4:** a 2-D majority-rule CA. Explore the ratio of binary states in the initial condition, the neighbourhood radius, and the number of states.

The majority rule shows **coarsening**: the grid starts noisy, and domains grow and merge until one state dominates. The slide figure uses a 100 x 100 grid, periodic boundary, radius 5.

## 3. Other CA types

- **Stochastic CA:** probabilistic state-transition rules.
- **Asynchronous CA:** cells are not all updated at once. Mechanisms are **random updating, sequential, and state-triggered**. They are deemed more robust and more applicable to real-world problems, since real systems have no global clock.
- **Neural CA:** see sections 5-7.

## 4. Example CA models

### 4a. Turing patterns

- 2-D grid, cells passive (0) or active (1).
- A cell activates if enough active cells are in its **local** neighbourhood. Active cells **farther out** suppress it, with weaker influence.
- This is **short-range activation and long-range inhibition**.
- **Formulas:**
  - N_a = {x' : |x'| <= R_a} and N_i = {x' : |x'| <= R_i}, with R_a < R_i.
  - a_t(x) = w_a · sum over N_a of s_t(x + x') - w_i · sum over N_i of s_t(x + x')
  - s_{t+1}(x) = 1 if a_t(x) > 0, else 0.
- **Result:** blob and stripe patterns, like animal coat patterns.
- **Exercise 11.6:** vary R_a, R_i and w_a, w_i and see how the pattern size and shape change.

### 4b. Waves in excitable media

- Models neural and muscle tissue, which can generate and propagate electrophysiological signals (action potentials).
- **States:** 0 = normal, 1 = excited, 2...k = **refractory** (the cell ignores stimuli).
- A normal cell gets excited by excited neighbours. After excitation it goes through the refractory states and back to 0.
- The refractory period gives **directionality** to signal propagation and creates **traveling waves**.
- **Exercise 11.7:** vary the excitation probability and the refractory period length.

### 4c. Host-pathogen

- **States:** 0 = empty, 1 = healthy host, 2 = infected host.
- A healthy host grows into nearby empty sites **stochastically**.
- A healthy host gets infected with a probability that is a **function of the number of infected neighbours**.
- An infected host dies (immediately or after some time), leaving the site empty.
- **Exercise 11.8:** vary the infection probability. Find the conditions for co-existence, host-wins and total extinction. Plot healthy and infected populations over time and look for temporal patterns.

### 4d. Epidemic / forest fire

- **States:** 0 = empty, 1 = tree, 2 = burning, 3 = char.
- Trees are placed with probability *p*. p = 0 means no trees and p = 1 means a full forest.
- Set one tree on fire. A tree catches fire if **at least one neighbour is burning**. A burning tree becomes char after one time step.
- **Exercise 11.9:** compare final results for different *p*. Plot **total burned area vs p** and **time until the fire stops vs p**.
- **Monte Carlo simulation:** run many independent replications per *p*, measure the outcome in each, and average. This gives a statistical distribution and more reliable results than a single run.
- *Not on the slides:* burned area typically jumps sharply at a critical *p* (the percolation threshold). That is another phase transition.

## 5. Why neural CA? Monolithic vs modular

- Deep learning and transformers are **monolithic** networks.
- The neocortex is built from ~2 x 10^8 **minicolumns**, many repeated local units. NCA follows this idea: one small local rule is applied everywhere.

## 6. Evolved Neural CA (CA-NEAT)

- S. Nichele, M. Ose, S. Risi, G. Tufte, *CA-NEAT: Evolved Compositional Pattern Producing Networks for Cellular Automata Morphogenesis and Replication*, IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems, 2018.
- The CA rule is a **CPPN** (Compositional Pattern Producing Network) **evolved with NEAT**.
- **Pipeline:** the 5-cell neighbourhood (centre + 4) is converted from discrete to continuous, passed through the evolved CPPN, then **select max** gives the output state.
- **Task:** morphogenesis, growing a target pattern (the "Tricolor" example) from a single seed cell.
- **Outcomes:** some solutions reach a **point attractor** equal to the target. Most found **cycles** instead. Some visit the target and then drift to a different attractor.

## 7. Google's Growing Neural CA

Sources: <https://distill.pub/2020/growing-ca/> and <https://distill.pub/2020/selforg/mnist/>. A **2-D, multichannel, continuous** CA.

| Component | What it does |
|---|---|
| **16 channels** | Each cell holds 16 values in [0, 1]. The first 4 are R, G, B, A. The rest are hidden channels. |
| **Moore neighbourhood** | 3 x 3 cells (9 cells). |
| **Perception** | Depthwise convolution with **Sobel-x, Sobel-y and identity** filters, concatenated into a perception vector. This lets a cell sense gradients and its own state. |
| **Network** | Dense-128, ReLU, Dense-16, outputting an update delta-s. |
| **Stochastic update** | Each cell randomly updates or not, so there is **no global synchronised clock** (a random interval between updates). |
| **Residual update** | delta-s is **added** to the current state. |
| **Alive masking** | Cells with no sufficiently alive neighbour (alpha below 0.1) are zeroed, so empty cells do not contribute. *The slide's wording "no alpha < 0.1" is a typo for "no alpha > 0.1".* |

**Three experiments:**

1. **Growing:** loss is the pixelwise RGBA difference to the target image. It is applied after a **random number of steps (64-96)**.
2. **Persistent:** you cannot just run for a very long time, so a **sample pool strategy** is used. States from earlier training iterations are re-used as seeds, and the **zygote** (initial seed) is always included. The goal is an **attractor state** that stays stable.
3. **Regenerate:** the structure is **damaged**, and the NCA learns to regrow it.

## 8. Bonus slides (explicitly *not* part of the syllabus)

Only a quick overview:

- **Cart-pole NCA** (Variengien, Pontes-Filho, Glover, Nichele, *Towards Self-organized Control: Using Neural Cellular Automata to Robustly Control a Cart-pole Agent*, Innovations in Machine Intelligence 2021): the NCA grid has input cells (4 physical parameters), output cells (expected reward for Left/Right, a Q-value) and intermediate cells. It has a **growing phase** (first ~50 steps) and a **control phase**, and it recovers after damage. 9 independent runs, 1000 time steps.
- **Neural Cellular Robot Substrate (GECCO 2022):** a single NCA that develops *and* controls a modular robot (body-brain co-evolution, light-chasing task). Pontes-Filho, Walker, Najarro, Nichele, Risi.
- **Spiking NCA for soft robots:** best paper at the ICLR 2022 workshop "From cells to societies, collective learning across scales".
- **EngramNCA** (memory transfer) and **ARC-NCA** (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus).
- **Quanta article:** reverse-engineering CA rules from target structures ("self-assembly gets automated in reverse of Game of Life").

**Next weeks (from the slides):** network theory and network models; presentation of group projects; agent-based models and evolutionary systems; the brain and biological neural network models.

## 9. Exam strategy

Expect questions like these:

- Explain the droplet rule, and why p = 0.1 vs 0.3 behave differently (phase transition).
- Compare synchronous and asynchronous CA, and stochastic CA.
- Describe the state diagrams of excitable media, host-pathogen and forest fire.
- Explain short-range activation and long-range inhibition (Turing patterns).
- Walk through the Growing NCA architecture (Sobel, dense layers, stochastic update, alive masking) and the three experiments.
- Explain why Monte Carlo is needed.

title: Network Models Part 1
reading:
## 1. Why networks?

- Networks are one of the newest developments in complex systems science, used in biology, ecology, sociology, economics, political science, management science, engineering, medicine and more (social, artificial neural, telecommunication and gene regulatory networks).
- **Two differences from cellular automata (CA):**
  1. Connectivity is **not uniform or regular**. Some nodes are very well connected and others are not, which makes the mathematics harder.
  2. The **number of components can change** over time in some dynamical network models.
- **Definition:** a network (graph) is a set of **nodes** (vertices, actors) plus a set of **edges** (links, ties).
- **Neighbour:** node *j* is a neighbour of *i* if and only if *i* is connected to *j*.

## 2. Representing a network

| Representation | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Adjacency matrix** | Matrix where a_ij = 1 if *i* and *j* are neighbours, else 0 |
| **Adjacency list** | For each node, the list of its neighbours (for example 3 -> {1, 2, 4}) |

- **Undirected graph:** the matrix is always **symmetric**.
- **Directed graph:** the matrix is generally **asymmetric**.
- **Weighted graph:** the matrix holds the weights instead of 0/1.

## 3. Vocabulary to know cold

- **Degree** deg(*i*): the number of edges at a node. **Node strength:** the sum of the weights of a node's edges, which equals the degree in unweighted graphs.
- **Walk:** a sequence of connected edges.
  - **Trail:** a walk with no repeated *edge*.
  - **Path:** a walk with no repeated *node* (so no repeated edge either).
  - **Cycle:** a walk that starts and ends at the same node, with no other repeated node.
- **Subgraph:** part of the graph.
- **Connected graph:** a path exists between every pair of nodes.
- **Connected component:** a subgraph that is connected internally but not to the rest of the graph.

**Named graph types:**

- **Complete:** every pair of nodes is connected.
- **Regular:** all nodes have the same degree. Every complete graph is regular.
- **Bipartite (n-partite):** nodes split into groups with no edge inside a group.
- **Tree:** no cycles. A forest is made of several trees. Every tree or forest is bipartite and planar.
- **Planar:** can be drawn in 2D with no edge crossings.

**Edge types:**

- **Undirected / directed:** symmetric or one-way.
- **Unweighted / weighted:** whether edges carry a value.
- **Multiple edges:** two nodes connected more than once.
- **Self-loop:** an edge from a node to itself.
- **Simple graph:** no directed, weighted or multiple edges and no self-loops.
- **Multigraph:** may contain multiple edges.
- **Hyperedge:** connects any number of nodes (hypergraph, not covered in the textbook).

## 4. NetworkX (Python)

- **Classes:**
  - `Graph`: undirected simple graph (self-loops allowed).
  - `DiGraph`: directed simple graph.
  - `MultiGraph`: undirected, multiple edges allowed.
  - `MultiDiGraph`: directed, multiple edges allowed.
- **Building a graph:** `add_node`, `add_nodes_from`, `add_edge`, `add_edges_from`, `remove_edge`, `remove_node`. Undefined nodes are created automatically when you add an edge. Removing a node removes its edges too.
- **Inspecting:** `g`, `g.nodes()`, `g.edges()`, node and edge attributes.
- **Ready-made graphs:** `complete_graph(5)`, `complete_bipartite_graph(3,4)`, `karate_club_graph()`.
- **Zachary's Karate Club:** the classic social network of friendships among 34 members of a karate club at a US university, reported by Wayne Zachary in the 1970s.
- **Random graphs:**
  - `gnm_random_graph(n, m)`: n nodes, m edges.
  - `gnp_random_graph(n, p)`: n nodes, edge probability p.
  - `random_regular_graph(d, n)`: n nodes, all of degree d.
  - `random_degree_sequence_graph([...])`: a given degree sequence.
- **Drawing:** `nx.draw(g)` with layouts (random, circular, spectral, shell, spring), plus node names, shapes, sizes and colours.
- **Import/export:** `nx.read_adjlist('file.csv', delimiter=',')`.
- **Version note:** the slide code uses the old API (`g.node[i]`, `g.edge`). In current NetworkX use `g.nodes[i]` and `g.edges`. The exam is conceptual, but this matters for projects.

## 5. Three kinds of dynamical network models

| Type | What changes |
|---|---|
| **Dynamics ON networks** | Node **states** change over time through interactions with connected nodes. Topology is **fixed**. |
| **Dynamics OF networks** | The **topology** changes over time (to study what creates topologies, robustness and vulnerability, or how to improve properties). |
| **Adaptive networks** | **Both**, co-evolving: states and topology adapt to each other. Many real-world systems behave like this. |

## 6. Simulating dynamics on networks

Implementation is very similar to CA, and often easier because neighbours are well defined. All of these use the same `initialize` / `observe` / `update` structure, run with PyCX.

### Local majority rule (`net-majority.py`)

- Nodes are individuals, edges are symmetric information-sharing links, and states are 0 or 1, initially random.
- Each node adopts the majority state in its **local neighbourhood, including itself**.
- Updates are **synchronous**, so you need a `nextg` copy of the graph.
- ratio = count / (degree + 1). If ratio > 0.5 the state becomes 1, if < 0.5 it becomes 0, and on a tie it is **random**.
- Result on the karate club: **two groups of different states form**.

### Voter model (discrete state/time model 1)

- A revision of the majority rule that is **asynchronous**: only **one opinion transfer per step**.
- Each node ("voter") holds one of a finite set of discrete states (for example a political opinion, red vs. blue).
- Variants:
  - **Original (pull):** pick a random *listener*, then a random *speaker* from its neighbours, and the listener copies the speaker.
  - **Reversed (push):** pick a random *speaker*, then a random *listener* from its neighbours.
  - **Edge-based (symmetric):** pick a random edge, then randomly assign its endpoints as speaker and listener.
- Code core (pull): `listener = choice(nodes)`, `speaker = choice(neighbors(listener))`, then `state[listener] = state[speaker]`.

### Epidemic model: SIS (discrete state/time model 2)

- Two states: **Susceptible** and **Infected**.
- **p_i** is the infection probability, with infection coming from infected neighbours. **p_r** is the recovery probability.
- An infected node stays infected with probability 1 - p_r. After recovery it is **susceptible again** (hence SIS). The alternative is **SIR**, where recovered nodes are removed or immune.
- Exercises 16.4 and 16.5 ask: vary p_i or p_r while fixing the other at 0.5. When does the disease persist (a "pandemic")? Is the transition gradual or sharp? How do network size and topology change this? (The lecture slides do not give answers, so run the simulation.)

## 7. Worked Exercise 15.1 (graph from the slide)

**Edges:** 1-2, 1-4, 1-5, 2-3, 2-4, 3-4, 3-5, 3-6, 4-6.

**1. Adjacency list:**

- 1 -> {2, 4, 5}
- 2 -> {1, 3, 4}
- 3 -> {2, 4, 5, 6}
- 4 -> {1, 2, 3, 6}
- 5 -> {1, 3}
- 6 -> {3, 4}

**Adjacency matrix** (rows and columns 1 to 6):

```
1: 0 1 0 1 1 0
2: 1 0 1 1 0 0
3: 0 1 0 1 1 1
4: 1 1 1 0 0 1
5: 1 0 1 0 0 0
6: 0 0 1 1 0 0
```

It is symmetric because the graph is undirected.

**2. Degrees:** deg(1)=3, deg(2)=3, deg(3)=4, deg(4)=4, deg(5)=2, deg(6)=2. The sum is 18, which is 2 x 9 edges. This is a handy sanity check.

**3. Walk classification:**

- 6-3-2-4-2-1: edge 2-4 is used twice and node 2 is repeated, so it is **just a walk (other)**.
- 1-4-6-3-2: no repeated node, so it is a **path** (and therefore also a trail).
- 5-1-2-3-5: starts and ends at 5 with no other repeats, so it is a **cycle**.

**4. Triangles:** {1,2,4}, {2,3,4} and {3,4,6}, so **3**. Check: {1,3,5} fails because 1-3 is not an edge.

**5. Remove nodes 3 and 4:** the edges 5-1 and 1-2 remain. The components are **{1,2,5}** and **{6}**, so 2 components.

## 8. Bonus material (not in syllabus)

Graph neural cellular automata (arXiv 2110.14237 and a blog post by Daniele Grattarola), a 2026 arXiv paper (2604.21446), and Stephen Wolfram's "Finally we may have a path to the fundamental theory of physics" (2020).

## 9. Exam strategy

- Be ready to **draw or convert** a graph to a matrix or list, compute degrees, and classify walks. These are the typical hands-on tasks.
- Know **dynamics on / of / adaptive** and give an example of each.
- Be able to explain **majority rule vs voter model** (synchronous vs asynchronous, deterministic vs random) and the **SIS parameters**.

The lecture has three parts: simulating dynamics on and of networks, then measuring networks with NetworkX.

## 1. Three kinds of dynamical network models

| Type | What changes | Topology |
|---|---|---|
| **Dynamics ON networks** | Node states change through interactions with neighbours | Fixed |
| **Dynamics OF networks** | The topology itself changes (to understand how topologies form, test robustness, or improve properties) | Changing |
| **Adaptive networks** | Both, co-evolving: states affect links and links affect states | Changing |

**Exam tip:** be able to give one example of each. The adaptive epidemic model is the standard adaptive example.

## 2. Simulating dynamics on networks

Implementation is very similar to cellular automata (CA), but "neighbours" are simpler to define on a network: they are the nodes connected by edges.

**Local majority rule (social network):**

- Nodes are individuals and edges are symmetric information-sharing links.
- Each state is 0 or 1, and initial states are random.
- Each node adopts the majority state in its neighbourhood, which includes itself.
- All nodes update **simultaneously**.

**SIS epidemic model** (discrete state and time):

- A **Susceptible** node is infected with probability **p_i** through infected neighbours.
- An **Infected** node recovers with probability **p_r**, and stays infected with 1 - p_r.
- A recovered node becomes **susceptible again**, so there is no immunity. In the **SIR** alternative, recovered nodes are immune.
- Book exercises:
  - **16.4:** vary p_i or p_r while fixing the other at 0.5, and find the condition under which the disease persists indefinitely. Check whether the transition is gradual or sharp.
  - **16.5:** try a larger network and other topologies, and see how size and topology affect persistence.

**Diffusion model** (continuous state and time):

- Each node's state moves toward its neighbours' average.
- The update is: `new c_i = c_i + alpha · (sum_j c_j - c_i · deg(i)) · dt`
- The term in parentheses is the sum over neighbours of (c_j - c_i). The state flows from high to low, like heat.
- **alpha** is the diffusion constant and **dt** is the time step. Over time all states converge toward gray, a common value.

## 3. Simulating dynamics of networks

1. **Small-world networks** are made by **random edge rewiring**. Start with a ring-like regular network and randomly rewire edges, which gives short paths while keeping high clustering.
2. **Scale-free networks** are made by **preferential attachment** (Barabási-Albert). New nodes prefer to connect to nodes that already have many links ("the rich get richer"). This gives a **power-law degree distribution** P(k) ~ k^(-gamma) (gamma = 3 in the lecture figure). It looks like a **straight line on log-log axes**, while on linear axes it is a steep drop with a long tail.

## 4. Adaptive networks

- **Adaptive SIS:** people avoid sick friends, so behaviour changes the topology, which changes how the disease spreads. A new parameter **p_s** controls how readily susceptible nodes cut links to infected neighbours. In Sayama's model they cut the link and rewire elsewhere. **Exercise 16.19** varies p_s (with p_i = 0.5, p_r = 0.2) to find when the disease is **eradicated**, then compares random, small-world and scale-free topologies. *(Open point flagged in the original chat: the exact mechanism of link cutting/rewiring in the adaptive SIS model should be verified against the book's Code 16.15.)*
- **Adaptive diffusion:** edge weights get **stronger or weaker depending on the state difference across the edge**. This models **homophily**, the tendency to connect with similar others. Result: the network splits into **separate clusters**, each with its own state (the figure shows a white group and a black group).

## 5. Network measures (NetworkX)

**Size and density**

- Size is the number of nodes n and edges m. The karate club graph has n = 34, m = 78.
- **Density** is the fraction of possible edges that exist: **rho = 2m / (n(n-1))** for undirected networks and **m / (n(n-1))** for directed ones. Karate club rho ≈ 0.139.
- Size and density do **not** determine topology: many different topologies share the same size and density.

**Percolation and giant components**

- Erdős-Rényi random graph: n nodes, each pair connected with probability p.
- A **giant component** is a connected component whose size is of the same order as the whole network.
- **Network percolation** is the appearance of a giant component, which happens when the **average degree is above 1**.
- In the n = 100 experiment, the transition happens at about **p ≈ 10^-2**. It goes from isolated nodes (p = 0.0001) to one giant network (p = 0.1).

**Shortest paths**

- d(i->j) is the shortest path length. It is symmetric in undirected networks but not in general for directed ones.
- Example: `nx.shortest_path_length(g, 16, 25)` gives 4, and the path is [16, 5, 0, 31, 25].
- **Characteristic path length** L = sum of d(i->j) / (n(n-1)), the average shortest path over all node pairs.
- **Eccentricity** eps(i) = max_j d(i->j), the distance to the farthest node.
- **Diameter** D = max eccentricity. Nodes with eps = D are **peripheries**.
- **Radius** R = min eccentricity. Nodes with eps = R are **centres**.

**Centrality** (who is most important?)

- **Degree centrality:** c_D(i) = deg(i) / (n-1)
- **Betweenness:** the probability that the shortest path between two random nodes passes through node i
- **Closeness** and **eigenvector** centrality
- **PageRank:** a variation of eigenvector centrality (Page and Brin, Google). It is the asymptotic probability that a random walker is standing on node i.

**Clustering (local property)**

- **C(i)** = actual links among i's neighbours divided by possible links, deg(i)(deg(i)-1)/2.
- It is the probability that i's neighbours are also neighbours of each other.
- It assumes an undirected network.
- Average clustering is C = sum of C(i) / n.

**Degree distribution**

- P(k) = (number of nodes with degree k) / n, the probability that a node has degree k.
- Karate club has a few high-degree hubs and many low-degree nodes. Scale-free networks follow a power law.

**Communities and modularity**

- A **community** is a set of nodes connected more densely to each other than to the rest.
- **Modularity** is the extent to which a network is organised into communities.
- There are many different ways to detect communities.

## 6. Likely exam angles

- Distinguish dynamics on, of and adaptive, with an example of each.
- Explain how SIS works, what p_i and p_r do, and how SIS differs from SIR.
- Explain why adaptive behaviour can eradicate a disease (links to infected nodes are cut).
- Explain how small-world and scale-free networks are generated.
- Compute density, and explain percolation and the giant component.
- Define eccentricity, diameter, radius and the characteristic path length formula.
- Compare the centrality measures.
- Interpret what C(i) means.
- Describe adaptive diffusion and homophily.

title: Agent-Based Models (ABM)
reading:
## 1. The big picture

An **agent-based model (ABM)** is a computational simulation with many discrete agents. You build many virtual individuals and simulate their behaviour explicitly on a computer. ABMs are one of the most general frameworks for complex systems, and they include **cellular automata and dynamical networks as special cases**.

**Agents:**

- Have internal properties (attributes such as position, age, knowledge, memory, experience, emotion)
- Are spatially localised and perceive the environment
- Interact locally with other agents and follow predefined rules
- Have **no central supervisor**
- May learn autonomously
- May produce non-trivial **collective behaviour** as a whole (emergence)

## 2. Developing an ABM (Macal & North, 2006)

1. Identify the agents and get a theory of agent behaviour
2. Identify agent relationships and get a theory of agent interaction
3. Get the requisite agent-related data
4. Validate the agent behaviour models and the model as a whole
5. Run the model and analyse the output

## 3. Approach A vs. approach B (very likely exam material)

| | **A** | **B** |
|---|---|---|
| Assumptions | Derived from empirically observed phenomena | Hypothetical |
| Goal | Produce previously unknown collective behaviour | Reproduce empirically observed collective phenomena |
| Use | **Make predictions** with validated theories | **Explore and develop new explanations** |
| Scales | Micro-known -> macro-unknown | Micro-unknown -> macro-known |

Memory hook: **A = predict, B = explain.**

## 4. Implementing an ABM

**Code steps:**

1. Choose a data format for each agent's properties
2. Create a population of agents in that format
3. Write code to visualise agent states, plus any analysis tools
4. Write code to update each agent's state according to the model's assumptions

**Six design tasks:**

1. Data structure for agent attributes
2. Data structure for environment states
3. Rules for how the environment behaves on its own
4. Rules for agent-environment interaction
5. Rules for how agents behave on their own
6. Rules for agent-agent interaction

**In Python:** a dynamic class works as a pure data structure (`class agent: pass`, then `a = agent(); a.x = 2; a.name = 'John'`).

Simulator structure (pycxsimulator): `initialize()`, `observe()`, `update()`.

## 5. Example models

### Schelling's segregation model

- Early 1970s, Thomas Schelling (2005 Nobel laureate in Economics). It is considered the first ABM.
- Built with **approach B**: hypothetical micro-rules reproduce the known macro-pattern of geographic segregation.
- **Rules:** two agent types in a finite 2-D space. Each iteration, a randomly chosen agent checks its neighbourhood. If the fraction of same-type neighbours is **below a threshold**, it jumps to a random location.
- **Code parameters:** `n = 1000` agents, `r = 0.1` neighbourhood radius, `th = 0.5` threshold.
- **Key finding:** segregation occurs even when the threshold is much lower than expected, so people do not need to be strongly homophilic.
- **Counter-intuitive:** very high homophily can produce a mixed society, because agents keep moving and never reach a stationary state.
- **Exercise 19.2:** vary `th`, `r`, `n` and find where segregation occurs. Is the transition gradual or sharp?

### Diffusion-limited aggregation (DLA)

- Two particle types: movable ones random-walk in 2-D, immovable ones stay put.
- **Only rule:** when a movable particle comes close enough to an immovable one, it becomes immovable forever.
- Start with one immovable seed in the centre, and a cluster pattern grows from it. With multiple seeds, clusters interact at macroscopic scales.

### Garbage collection by ants (Resnick, *Turtles, Termites and Traffic Jams*)

- Ants wander randomly. If an ant holds garbage, it drops it. If it holds nothing, it picks some up.
- This is an agent-**environment** interaction (the garbage lives in the environment).
- **Result:** the ants spontaneously collect and pile up garbage and clear the space. This is emergent behaviour that runs against intuition.

### Birth/death of agents

The update procedure must:

- Decide whether each current agent survives. If yes, update its state. If no, remove it from the list.
- Simulate births. New agents are added to the list at the end.

### Predator-prey model

- Rabbits and foxes wander and reproduce. Foxes move faster.
- A rabbit survives if it is not caught. A fox survives if it ate recently. Fox reproduction depends on successful eating.
- Population curves **oscillate**, and extinction of predators (or both) can occasionally happen.
- **Exercise 19.9:** make coexistence more robust. **Exercise 19.10:** add grass as a third species.

### Evolution in ABMs (evolvable predator-prey)

Three components:

- **Inheritance:** offspring have attributes similar to their parents'
- **Variation:** diversity in attributes, mainly from imperfect inheritance (mutation)
- **Selection:** different attributes give different survivability (fitness)

When all three are present, evolution can occur in **any** system: biological, social, cultural or informational. Exercises 19.11-19.13 cover evolving the movement magnitude `m` and later the reproduction rates.

The bonus links (an arXiv paper and OpenAI's Neural MMO) are marked as extra material, so they are unlikely to be core exam content.

## 6. Practice beyond the quiz

- **Exercise 19.2 and 19.8:** be ready to explain what you would vary and what you would expect to see.
- **A vs. B:** be able to classify a new model as predictive (A) or explanatory (B) and justify it with the micro-known / macro-unknown framing.

> **Note:** in the original chat the student labelled this "Lecture 5", but the attached PDF was Lecture 6 (agent-based models). It is filed here as Lecture 6.
